segments.text: Sonae. The agent team that stands watch over your family. Built on the Strands Agents SDK and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.

Japan asks every household to prepare a personal evacuation timeline: who does what, at which official alert level. That means reading the hazard map for your address, learning which evacuation site is designated for which disaster, and agreeing it with your family. It is homework assigned to every household in Japan, and it waits until the river is rising.

The people least able to do it are the ones who die. In Japan's recent floods, sixty five to eighty percent of the dead were aged sixty five or over. Often a parent, alone in the family home, hours away from their children.

Typhoon Hagibis, twenty nineteen. At half past three in the afternoon, the first emergency heavy rain warning ever issued for Nagano Prefecture. The evacuation order for the riverside came at twenty three forty, in darkness and driving rain. After one in the morning the river came over the bank at Hoyasu, and the district flooded to the rooftops. The information was public the whole time.

This is Sonae. One address, and a few sentences about your family. A Cartographer reads the statutory hazard maps. A Planner drafts the timeline, tuned to a grandmother's knees. An adversarial Verifier re-derives every claim from the same official data. You approve it once, calmly. From here, Sonae is authorized to act.
October eleventh, replayed minute by minute from the official record. The day before landfall: level one. Charge the phone. Pack the medication. While the sky is clear.

Saturday afternoon, the river reaches advisory levels. Level two. And here the verifier earns its keep. The draft told the son to skip level three and escalate immediately to level three. A contradiction, in an instruction someone reads while frightened. Rejected, corrected, then sent.

Half past three. The emergency heavy rain warning. Formally that is level five for rainfall, but level five means protect yourself where you are, and the guidance is to finish evacuating while you still can. So Sonae pushes the plan's level four step, a rule the family approved in advance. Complete the evacuation now. The first draft called it an evacuation order. No municipality had issued one. Rejected, corrected, then sent, in each reader's own language. Sunset is at seventeen sixteen. There is still light to walk in.

Then, discipline. Bulletins the plan already covers. The Sentinel stands by through all of them. It is not always right on its own: elsewhere in this journal, on this same six o'clock advisory, it claimed level five, and a deterministic guard clamped it back to four. A model does not get the last word on how frightened your family should be.
Eight fifty PM. Upstream, the river comes over its left bank. Level five. Confirm everyone is out, and that nobody goes back in. Safety check-ins open on every phone.

Twenty three forty. The emergency evacuation order — the moment the real residents of Hoyasu were told to leave. At eight minutes past one, the river came over the bank at their doorstep. Sonae's verified push had gone out eight hours and nine minutes earlier. On the plan's own walking allowance, Yoshiko is at the shelter before six in the evening.

After the water, Japanese neighborhoods confirm safety with paper name lists, carried door to door. Sonae's circle mode replaces the paper, not the neighbors, and tells the chairman which door to knock on first: the eighty eight year old, still unconfirmed.

None of this is staged. Every line here is quoted from the journal committed in the repository. AI prose fails closed: unverified text is never sent. The official signal fails open: relayed verbatim rather than silenced. And the family's approval is the authorization boundary.

Under the hood, a self-correcting Strands graph builds the plan and a verified pipeline runs the watch, with typed JSON between agents and flight recorder hooks on every tool call. It runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore: deployed, state synced to S3, an EventBridge heartbeat. On a calm day a watch cycle costs zero model tokens. Boring is the job.

All of it runs on public government data. Built for Japan, portable to any country that publishes its hazards. Sonae. Because the next Hagibis is already forming, and every family deserves someone on watch.
